slots.text: If there were no eternal consciousness in a human being; if at the bottom of everything there lay only a wildly seething power that, writhing in dark passions, brought forth everything, both what was great and what was insignificant; if a bottomless emptiness, never satisfied, lay hidden beneath everything — what then would life be but despair? If that were how things stood; if there were no sacred bond that tied humankind together; if one generation rose up after another like the leaves in the forest; if one generation succeeded another like the birdsong in the forest; if the human race passed through the world as a ship passes through the sea, as the wind passes through the desert, a thoughtless and fruitless labor; if an eternal oblivion, always hungry, lay in wait for its prey, and there were no power strong enough to wrest it away — how empty and comfortless life would be! But for that very reason it is not so. As God created man and woman, so he formed the hero and the poet or orator. The poet can do nothing of what the hero does; he can only admire the hero, love him, rejoice in him. Yet he too is happy, no less than the hero. For the hero is, so to speak, his better self, the self he is in love with — and he is glad that it is not, after all, he himself, so that his love can be admiration. He is the genius of recollection. He can do nothing but call to mind what has been done, nothing but admire what has been done; he takes nothing from what is his own, but he guards jealously what has been entrusted to him. He follows his heart’s choice; but once he has found what he sought, he goes about from door to door with his song and with his speech, so that all may admire the hero as he does, and be proud of the hero as he is. This is his exploit, his humble labor; this is his loyal service in the hero’s household. If he stays true to his love in this way, if he contends day and night with the wiles of oblivion, which would cheat him of his hero, then he has accomplished his labor. Then he is united with the hero, who has loved him no less faithfully; for the poet is, so to speak, the hero’s better self — powerless, certainly, as a memory is, but also transfigured, as a memory is. That is why none who were great shall be forgotten. And even if it takes a long time, even if the cloud of misunderstanding carries the hero away, his lover still comes; and the more time has passed, the more faithfully he clings to him.

No! No one who was great in the world shall be forgotten. But each was great in his own fashion, and each according to the greatness of what he loved. For the one who loved himself became great through himself, and the one who loved other people became great through his devotion; but the one who loved God became greater than all. Each shall be remembered, but each became great according to his expectation. One became great through expecting the possible, another through expecting the eternal; but the one who expected the impossible became greater than all. Each shall be remembered, but each was great according to the magnitude of what he strove with. For the one who strove with the world became great through overcoming the world, and the one who strove with himself became greater through overcoming himself; but the one who strove with God became greater than all. Thus there was strife in the world, man against man, one against a thousand; but the one who strove with God was greater than all. Thus there was strife on the earth: there was one who overcame everything through his power, and there was one who overcame God through his powerlessness. There was one who trusted in himself and won everything; there was one who, secure in his strength, sacrificed everything; but the one who believed God was greater than all. There was one who was great through his power, and one great through his wisdom, and one great through his hope, and one great through his love; but Abraham was greater than all — great through that power whose strength is powerlessness, great through that wisdom whose secret is foolishness, great through that hope whose form is madness, great through that love which is hatred of oneself.

By faith Abraham journeyed out of the land of his fathers and became a foreigner in the land of promise. He left one thing behind and took one thing with him: he left his earthly understanding behind, and he took faith with him. Otherwise he would surely not have journeyed out, but would have thought: this is, after all, preposterous. By faith he was a foreigner in the land of promise, and there was nothing there that reminded him of what was dear to him; instead, everything, by its newness, tempted his soul to wistful longing. And yet he was God’s chosen one, in whom the Lord delighted! Indeed, had he been an outcast, thrust away from God’s grace, he could have understood it better; as things were, it seemed to mock him and his faith. There was also one in the world who lived in exile from his fathers’ land, which he loved. He is not forgotten, nor are his laments, when in his wistfulness he sought and found what was lost. Of Abraham there is no lament. It is human to lament, human to weep with the one who weeps; but it is greater to have faith, more blessed to behold the believer.

By faith Abraham received the promise that in his seed all the families of the earth would be blessed. Time went by, the possibility was there, Abraham believed; time went by, it became preposterous, Abraham believed. There was one in the world who also had an expectation. Time went by, evening drew on; he was not so paltry as to have forgotten his expectation, and therefore he shall not be forgotten either. Then he grieved, and his grief did not deceive him as life had done; it did for him everything it could, and in the sweetness of grief he possessed his disappointed expectation. It is human to grieve, it is human to grieve with the one who grieves; but it is greater to have faith, more blessed to behold the believer. Of Abraham we have no song of grief. He did not wistfully count the days as the seasons went by; he did not look at Sarah with suspicious glances, watching whether she was growing old; he did not halt the course of the sun so that Sarah would not age, and his expectation with her; he did not sing his wistful song to Sarah to lull her. Abraham grew old, Sarah became an object of mockery in the land; and yet he was God’s chosen one and heir to the promise that in his seed all the families of the earth would be blessed. Would it not, then, have been better if he had not been God’s chosen one? What does it mean to be God’s chosen one? Is it to be denied in youth the wish of youth, and then, with great hardship, to have it fulfilled in old age? But Abraham believed and kept hold of the promise. Had Abraham wavered, he would have given it up; he would have said to God: “So perhaps it is not your will, after all, that it should happen; then I will give up the wish. It was my only wish, it was my blessedness. My soul is sincere; I harbor no secret resentment because you denied it.” He would not have been forgotten; by his example he would have saved many; yet he would not have become the father of faith. For it is great to give up one’s wish, but it is greater to keep hold of it once one has given it up; it is great to grasp the eternal, but it is greater to keep hold of the temporal once one has given it up. — Then the fullness of time came. Had Abraham not believed, Sarah would probably have died of grief, and Abraham, dulled by heartache, would not have understood the fulfillment but would have smiled at it as at a youthful dream. But Abraham believed; therefore he was young. For the one who always hopes for the best grows old, deceived by life; and the one who is always ready for the worst grows old before his time; but the one who believes keeps an eternal youth. Praised be that story, then! For Sarah, though advanced in years, was young enough to desire a mother’s joy, and Abraham, though his hair was gray, was young enough to want to be a father. Outwardly, the wonder lies in its having happened as they expected; in a deeper sense, the wonder of faith lies in this: that Abraham and Sarah were young enough to wish, and that faith had kept their wish, and with it their youth. He received the fulfillment of the promise; he received it believing, and it happened according to the promise and according to faith. For Moses struck the rock with his staff, but he did not believe.
Then there was joy in Abraham’s house, when Sarah stood as a bride on their golden wedding day.

Yet it was not to remain so; once more Abraham was to be put to the proof. He had fought with that cunning power that invents everything, with that watchful enemy that never slumbers, with that old man who survives everything — he had fought with time and held on to his faith. Now all the terror of the fight was concentrated into a single moment. “And God tempted Abraham and said to him: Take Isaac, your only son, the one you love, and go to the land of Moriah and offer him up there as a burnt offering on a mountain I will show you.”

So everything was lost, more terribly than if it had never happened! So the Lord was only mocking Abraham! Wondrously he had made the preposterous real; now he wanted to see it brought to nothing again. It was, to be sure, foolishness; but Abraham did not laugh at it, as Sarah had laughed when the promise was announced. Everything was lost! Seventy years of faithful expectation, the brief joy at faith’s fulfillment. Who is it, then, who snatches the staff from the old man? Who is it who demands that he break it himself! Who is it who makes a man’s gray hairs comfortless? Who is it who demands that he do it himself! Has no one pity for the venerable old man, none for the innocent child! And yet Abraham was God’s chosen one, and it was the Lord who laid the test on him. Everything was now to be lost! The glorious remembrance of the generations, the promise in Abraham’s seed — it was only a whim, a fleeting thought the Lord had had, which Abraham was now to wipe out. That glorious treasure, just as old as the faith in Abraham’s heart and older by many, many years than Isaac, the fruit of Abraham’s life, hallowed by prayers, ripened in struggles — the blessing on Abraham’s lips — this fruit was now to be wrenched off before its time and lose its meaning; for what meaning did it have, if Isaac was to be sacrificed! That wistful yet blessed hour when Abraham was to take leave of everything dear to him, when he would lift his venerable head once more, when his face would shine like the Lord’s, when he would gather his whole soul into a blessing powerful enough to make Isaac blessed all his days — that hour was not to come! For Abraham was indeed to part from Isaac, but so that he himself stayed behind; death was to separate them, but so that Isaac became its prey. The old man was not to lay his hand on Isaac in blessing, gladly, in death, but, weary of life, to lay violent hands on Isaac. And it was God who tested him. Yes, woe! Woe to the messenger who had come before Abraham with such tidings! Who would have dared to be the envoy of this sorrow? But it was God who tested Abraham.

Yet Abraham believed, and believed for this life. Indeed, if his faith had been only for a life to come, he would surely have found it easier to cast everything away, in order to hurry out of a world where he did not belong. But Abraham’s faith was not of that kind, if there is such a kind at all. For that is not really faith but faith’s most distant possibility, which senses its object dimly at the farthest edge of the horizon, yet is separated from it by a yawning abyss in which despair plays its game. But Abraham believed precisely for this life: that he would grow old in the land, honored among the people, blessed in his descendants, never to be forgotten in Isaac, the dearest thing in his life. He embraced Isaac with a love for which it was only a poor expression to say that he faithfully fulfilled a father’s duty to love his son — as indeed the summons itself puts it: the son whom you love. Jacob had twelve sons and one whom he loved; Abraham had only one, whom he loved.

But Abraham believed and did not doubt; he believed the preposterous. If Abraham had doubted — he would then have done something else, something great and glorious; for how could Abraham do anything that was not great and glorious! He would have gone out to Mount Moriah, he would have split the wood, lit the fire, drawn the knife — he would have cried out to God: “Do not scorn this sacrifice. It is not the best thing I have, I know that well; for what is an old man beside the child of promise? Yet it is the best I have to give you. Let Isaac never find out, so that he may take comfort in his youth.” He would have driven the knife into his own breast. The world would have admired him, and his name would not have been forgotten; but to be admired is one thing, to become a guiding star that saves the anxious is another.
But Abraham believed. He did not pray for himself, that he might move the Lord; it was only when the just punishment went out over Sodom and Gomorrah that Abraham came forward with his prayers.

We read in those holy scriptures: “And God tempted Abraham, and said: Abraham, Abraham, where are you? But Abraham answered: Here I am.” You to whom my speech is addressed, was that how it was with you? When you saw the heavy visitations of fate approaching from far off, did you not then say to the mountains, “Hide me,” and to the hills, “Fall upon me”? Or were you stronger — even so, did your foot not move slowly along the road, did it not long, as it were, to go back along the old tracks? When you were called, did you answer, or did you not answer — perhaps softly, in a whisper? Not so Abraham. Gladly, boldly, trustingly, loudly he answered: Here I am. We read further: “And Abraham rose early in the morning.” He hurried as though he were going to a festival, and early in the morning he was at the place agreed, on Mount Moriah. He told Sarah nothing, Eliezer nothing; and who could have understood him anyway? Had not the temptation, by its very nature, taken from him a vow of silence? “He split the wood, he bound Isaac, he lit the fire, he drew the knife.” My listener! Many a father believed that in his child he was losing what was dearest to him in the world, and being robbed of every hope for the future; yet surely none was a child of promise in the sense in which Isaac was so for Abraham. Many a father lost his child; but then it was God, the unchangeable and unsearchable will of the Almighty — his hand took it. Not so with Abraham. For him a harder test was reserved, and Isaac’s fate was laid, together with the knife, in Abraham’s hand. There he stood, the old man, with his one hope! Yet he did not doubt, did not glance anxiously right or left, did not challenge heaven with his prayers. He knew it was God the Almighty who was testing him; he knew this was the hardest sacrifice that could be required of him; but he also knew that no sacrifice was too hard when God required it — and he drew the knife.

Who strengthened Abraham’s arm, who held his right hand raised so that it did not sink down powerless! Whoever looks at this is paralyzed. Who strengthened Abraham’s soul, so that his eyes did not go dark and he saw neither Isaac nor the ram! Whoever looks at this goes blind. — And yet rare enough, perhaps, is the one who is paralyzed and blinded; rarer still is the one who tells worthily what happened. We all know it — it was only a test.

If Abraham, as he stood on Mount Moriah, had doubted; if he had looked about him at a loss; if, before he drew the knife, he had caught sight of the ram by chance; if God had let him sacrifice it in Isaac’s place — then he would have gone home and all would have been as before: he would have had Sarah, he would have kept Isaac, and yet how changed! For his return would have been a flight, his rescue a matter of chance, his reward shame, his future perhaps perdition. Then he would have testified neither to his faith nor to God’s grace, but to how terrible it is to go up to Mount Moriah. Then Abraham would not have been forgotten, nor Mount Moriah either. It would then be named — not as Ararat is named, where the Ark came to land, but named as a terror, because it was here that Abraham doubted.

Venerable Father Abraham! When you went home from Mount Moriah, you had no need of a eulogy to comfort you for your loss; for you won everything and kept Isaac — was it not so? The Lord did not take him from you again; instead you sat at table with him, glad, in your tent, as you do in the world beyond for all eternity. Venerable Father Abraham! Millennia have rolled by since those days, yet you need no late-coming lover to snatch your memory from the power of oblivion; for every tongue calls you to mind — and yet you reward your lover more splendidly than any other: in the world beyond you make him blessed in your bosom; here you hold his eye and his heart captive by the wonder of your deed. Venerable Father Abraham! Second father of the race! You who first felt and bore witness to that tremendous passion which scorns the terrible fight with the raging of the elements and the forces of creation in order to strive with God; you who first knew that highest passion, the holy, pure, humble expression of the divine madness that the pagans admired — forgive the one who wanted to speak in your praise, if he has not done it rightly. He spoke humbly, as his heart desired; he spoke briefly, as is fitting. But he will never forget that you needed a hundred years to get a son of your old age against all expectation, that you had to draw the knife before you could keep Isaac; he will never forget that in a hundred and thirty years you got no further than faith.
